notes.summary: The journey from Nand to Tetris starts with one gate and a rule: every chip in the course is specified by an API (interface) and implemented in HDL by composing other chips. You build Not, And, Or, Mux, Dmux and the bus versions from nothing but Nand. The hardware simulator grades you — behavior, not syntax, is what counts.
notes.focus: Derive Not from Nand on paper before typing any HDL. If you can prove it with Boolean algebra, the remaining gates are variations.

notes.summary: Adders from logic gates: half adder (sum + carry), full adder (carry-in), and the ripple 16-bit adder. The centerpiece is the Hack ALU — which computes arithmetic by bitwise trickery (negation flags) rather than dedicated circuits. Building it proves computation is just logic, and it's the heart of the computer you'll assemble in project 5.
notes.focus: The ALU's zx/nx/zy/ny/f/no bits look cryptic — work the truth table for a few flag combinations until each bit's job is obvious.

notes.summary: Time enters the machine: DFFs (given) make bits persist, registers stack a bit behind a load gate, and RAM is an array of registers addressed by a mux/demux tree. You build the program counter — the register that jumps. Clock discipline from 6.004 returns here, but now you build the state hardware yourself.
notes.focus: Write RAM8's HDL by composing registers with an 8-way mux. Address decoding is the pattern; get it right once at small scale and RAM16K is identical.

notes.summary: You program the Hack computer before it exists: the 16-bit instruction set (A-instructions set addresses, C-instructions compute), the three pseudo-commands, and the CPU emulator. Writing multiplication and I/O programs in raw assembly builds the mental model that makes the assembler (project 6) and the VM translator (projects 7-8) obvious.
notes.focus: Hand-simulate a loop in the CPU emulator, watching the PC and A register. When the jump mechanism clicks, the whole machine language becomes readable.

practice.title: Build the CPU and the Hack computer

notes.summary: The summit of the hardware half: you wire the ALU, registers, and PC into a complete CPU, then attach ROM32K, RAM16K, screen, and keyboard into the Hack computer — a stored-program machine you built gate by gate. Running your project-4 assembly ON your project-5 computer is one of the great moments in this entire study path.
concepts: The von Neumann cycle in HDL
notes.focus: Decode one C-instruction field by field and trace the control bits to the parts they drive. The CPU is just a decoder wired to components you already trust.

notes.summary: The software half begins: a two-pass assembler that parses Hack assembly, resolves symbols (labels and variables), and emits binary. It's your first real translator program, and its architecture — parse, symbol table, code generation — is exactly the shape of the Jack compiler you build in projects 10-11.
notes.focus: Build the parser first with unit tests on tiny programs. The two passes are easy to conflate — keeping them separate is what makes the code clean.

lecture.title: Nand2Tetris Project 7: VM Translator — Stack Arithmetic

notes.summary: The virtual machine concept: compilers target an abstract stack machine, and the VM translator lowers push/pop/arithmetic commands into Hack assembly. You implement the command parser and code writer for arithmetic and logical operations. This two-tier compilation design is how Java, .NET, and WebAssembly all work.
notes.focus: Write the assembly template for 'add' by hand first — then your code writer just stamps it. Template thinking makes translation programs almost boring, which is the point.

lecture.title: Nand2Tetris Project 8: VM Translator — Program Control

notes.summary: The VM's hard core: branching (label/goto/if-goto), functions with arguments and locals, and the call/return protocol that pushes frames. The generated bootstrap code starts the ball rolling. Recursion works when this works — which means your 6.100L-era mental model of stack frames is now something you EMIT.
notes.focus: Trace one VM call through your generated assembly with the VM emulator. Watching a recursive Fibonacci stack grow in code YOU generated is the payoff.

notes.summary: A taste of the other side: Jack, a simple Java-like OO language you will soon compile. You write a small application (a game or tool) in Jack and run it on the platform you built. Using your own machine as a user reveals exactly what a language needs: classes, methods, arrays, strings — and what a compiler must handle.
notes.focus: Write something fun and small (a Snake game). You'll hit every language feature naturally, which is exactly the test suite your compiler needs.

notes.summary: Compilation begins: the tokenizer turns Jack source into a token stream, and a recursive-descent parser validates it against the Jack grammar, emitting an XML parse tree. This is the same front-end architecture Stanford's CS143 formalizes — you are building it two terms early, at toy scale, by hand.
notes.focus: Map each grammar rule to one parsing function. When the grammar and code look identical in shape, you have written a parser the way professionals do.

practice.title: Emit VM code from the parse tree

notes.summary: The compiler's back end: walk the parse tree and emit VM code — expressions as stack operations, variables as segments, methods as functions with this as argument zero, and objects as heap blocks. String literals, symbol tables with scope, and the standard library's implicit calls complete the pipeline from Jack source to running program.
notes.focus: Compile a hello-world Jack program and run the pipeline end to end: your compiler, your VM translator, your hardware. Trace one print statement the whole way down.

practice.title: Build the Jack OS: memory, screen, keyboard

notes.summary: Project 12 is the OS half checkpoint: the Jack runtime library — memory management (alloc/free with a free list), screen drawing (line, circle, text), keyboard input, string and Math routines — all written in Jack itself. You are writing the layer your compiler's programs depend on, and discovering that an OS is just a library with privileges.
notes.focus: Implement Memory.alloc with a first-fit free list and draw the heap's state after a scripted alloc/free sequence. That picture is a real malloc in miniature.

practice.title: Finish the OS and run Tetris

notes.summary: The finish line: with the OS complete, the full toolchain — hardware, assembler, VM translator, compiler, OS — runs the course's Tetris game, every layer built by you. Review the full stack bottom-up, then write the one-page diagram of how a Jack statement becomes a gate transition. That diagram is your ticket to 6.1810's xv6 next.
concepts: What an OS kernel really is
notes.focus: Play the Tetris game you compiled on the machine you built. Then write that one-page stack diagram from memory — it is the course, compressed.
